The core idea is compelling: **edit your real config files, get automatic history, recover mistakes, and carry the setup to another machine.** The post explains that well initially, but then becomes a feature manual. I’d make a substantial editorial cut before publishing.

1. **Lead with the payoff the title promises.** The opening jumps to `bootstrap --from-git`, which is about restoring a setup. Tracking → editing → automatic save → rollback is the stronger opening demonstration. Move the new-machine command after readers understand what was saved.

2. **Keep the personal voice; trim the implementation tour.** The rcm story and video-game analogy give this a reason to exist. The Claude command, Git repository internals, remote relay flags, throttling rules, and hardware-key limitations compete with that story. Move most of those into linked docs. Aim to cut roughly a third.

3. **Make automatic sync explicit.** “With automatic sync enabled” leaves me wondering whether I need to enable it; later you call it the default. State the default where origin is introduced. Also distinguish local autosave from publishing early enough that readers understand what connecting a remote changes.

4. **Tighten “One repository for your setup.”** This is the densest section. The autosquash speculation, bare-repository explanation, raw Git command, retention warning, conflict behavior, notification limitations, and rollback semantics need more separation—or fewer details. Keep the essentials: saves stay local until connected, sync shares committed history, conflicts pause sharing, and live files don’t get conflict markers.

5. **Give encryption its own short section.** It’s buried under “Not every file should behave the same way,” alongside noisy files and OS variants. Keep encryption-before-Git, visible filenames, old plaintext history, and recovery keys. The TPM/Secure Enclave discussion is documentation material. Also explicitly say the live restored file remains plaintext; readers shouldn’t have to infer that.

6. **Remove speculative asides that interrupt the explanation.** “I may change that functionality…” and “I may tweak this behavior…” make the workflow sound unsettled without helping readers use it. Your candid voice works better when describing the actual tradeoff: automatic sync can stall on conflicts, and you rely on notifications to notice.

7. **State availability and prerequisites.** Which mise version includes this? Is it experimental? The post should answer those before the first tutorial command. The opening complaint about needing Git authentication also deserves a clearer resolution: local bootstrap still requires it; the relay addresses remote provisioning.

The strongest material is the rollback-and-undo example, tracking files without moving them, and the explanation that tracking the mise config brings the rest of the setup along. Those are concrete, memorable benefits.

I’d organize it as: **personal problem → track and autosave → recover a mistake → sync → bootstrap another machine → brief optional features → try it.** That would make the title’s promise the spine of the article instead of one feature among many.

This is an editorial critique of the [PR’s Markdown](https://github.com/jdx/blog/pull/99), not a verification of the implementation or rendered preview.

**I found no match among the established dotfile managers I checked—but I did find a small, close precedent: [Tether CLI](https://github.com/paddo-tech/tether-cli), with 12 stars.** So “unusual among established dotfile managers” is supported; “nobody has done this” is too strong.

Tether’s daemon periodically pulls Git changes, decrypts and writes ordinary dotfiles in their original locations, captures local changes, commits, and pushes. I checked its [daemon implementation](https://github.com/paddo-tech/tether-cli/blob/main/src/daemon/server.rs) and [file application code](https://github.com/paddo-tech/tether-cli/blob/main/src/cli/commands/sync.rs), beyond its marketing claims.

The matrix below compares **built-in background behavior**, after configuration. Running explicit commands or adding your own scripts/scheduler doesn’t count as automatic. Stars are GitHub counts checked September 7, 2026; mise follows your 2026.9.2 release assumption.

| Project · stars | Live-file model | Automatically captures live edits into Git | Automatically publishes changes | Automatically fetches and applies incoming changes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **[mise](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/12919) · 33.6k¹** | Ordinary files in place | **Yes, filesystem watcher** | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| [chezmoi](https://www.chezmoi.io/user-guide/setup/) · 21.5k | Ordinary files generated/copied from sources | No ambient target-file watcher | On chezmoi commands² | Explicit `chezmoi update` |
| [yadm](https://yadm.io/docs/getting_started) · 6.4k | Ordinary files tracked directly | Explicit commits | Explicit push | Explicit pull |
| [vcsh](https://github.com/RichiH/vcsh) · 2.3k | Ordinary files tracked directly | Explicit commits | Explicit push | Explicit pull |
| [GNU Stow](https://www.gnu.org/software/stow/) / [Dotbot](https://github.com/anishathalye/dotbot) · — / 8k | Symlinks | External Git workflow | External | External |
| [Dotdrop](https://github.com/deadc0de6/dotdrop) · 1.9k | Copies/templates; optional symlinks | Explicit update and commit | Explicit Git push | Explicit pull and install |
| [Dotter](https://github.com/SuperCuber/dotter) · 2k | Symlinks/templates | No; watcher deploys **repository → target** | External | External |
| [Mackup](https://github.com/lra/mackup) · 15.3k | Copies or symlinks | No built-in Git capture | Cloud sync in **symlink mode** | Cloud sync in **symlink mode** |
| **[Tether](https://tether-cli.com/docs#how-it-works) · 12** | Ordinary dotfiles; encrypted repository copies | **Yes, five-minute polling** | **Yes** | **Yes** |
| [gitwatch](https://github.com/gitwatch/gitwatch#what-it-does) · 1.7k | Ordinary files within a Git repository | Yes | Optional automatic push | No documented incoming-sync loop |

¹ Mise’s stars belong to the whole project, not adoption of this feature.

² Chezmoi supports `autoCommit` and `autoPush` when its commands change source state. Its documented [Watchman integration](https://www.chezmoi.io/user-guide/advanced/use-chezmoi-with-watchman/) watches the **source directory** and applies changes; it doesn’t provide the complete live-file-to-other-machine cycle. [Configuration reference](https://www.chezmoi.io/reference/configuration-file/variables/#git).

A few smaller projects help establish where the boundaries are:

- **[DFS](https://github.com/charlesrocket/dfs), 7 stars:** watches and synchronizes local source files/templates and live files in both directions. Its daemon’s synchronization path doesn’t implement the automatic Git publication and retrieval loop.
- **[etcdotica](https://github.com/senotrusov/etcdotica), 19 stars:** also provides continuous local two-way copying with `-collect -watch`; remote Git synchronization is separate.
- **[Workbench](https://github.com/mxcl/Workbench), 666 stars:** automatic dotfile backup to iCloud, but explicitly says it supports only one computer.

There are also substantial precedents outside dotfile managers. **[Syncthing](https://docs.syncthing.net/users/syncing.html)** already synchronizes ordinary files automatically in both directions. Its optional versioning archives files replaced by incoming changes, rather than recording every local edit. **[SparkleShare](https://github.com/hbons/SparkleShare)**, with 4,982 stars, already provides automatic bidirectional Git synchronization inside managed folders. Those make a broad claim about inventing automatic file synchronization—or automatic Git synchronization—untenable.

**What distinguishes mise most clearly is the integrated workflow.** It combines watching native files, local history independent of an origin, automatic cross-machine Git synchronization, and labeled before/after captures with undo. That sits alongside mise’s existing deployment models and tools/packages/services bootstrap. Tether already overlaps on encryption, profiles, package syncing, and history, so those features individually aren’t unique either. [Mise history implementation and documentation](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/12919), [Tether documentation](https://tether-cli.com/docs).

I would phrase the post like this:

> I wanted automatic two-way syncing of the files I actually edit, with Git history and no symlinks. I couldn’t find that combination in an established dotfile manager, so I added it to mise.

And I’d avoid presenting symlinks and generated files as an exhaustive taxonomy: **yadm and vcsh already manage ordinary live files directly.** The distinctive addition is making the complete save-and-sync cycle happen automatically.
